name: Old French
notes: Skeleton. Old French (c. 842-1400). Retains the affricate values ⟨ch⟩=/tʃ/, ⟨j/g⟩=/dʒ/, ⟨c/ç⟩=/ts/, ⟨z⟩=/ts/ that later simplified; final dental spirants (⟨t⟩=/θ/) occur early. Diphthongs and nasal vowels are only partially recoverable from spelling. POSITIONAL READINGS: ⟨c⟩ and ⟨g⟩ before ⟨e i⟩ are /ts/ and /dʒ/, which is why ⟨qu⟩ and ⟨gu⟩ had to be kept for /k/ and /ɡ/ in that same position (Schwan & Behrens §13); word-internal intervocalic ⟨s⟩ is voiced /z/ while the spelling stays ⟨s⟩ (§126.1). Geminate ⟨ss⟩ stays voiceless (§127) and is not intervocalic by the engine's test, so the ⟨s⟩ entry leaves it alone. ⟨ü⟩ is ⟨u⟩ = /y/ carrying the editors' hiatus diaeresis (armeüre [aɾməyɾə]); without the key the letter has no reading at any length and the tokenizer drops it silently. NO graphemes_base: the parent la-x-gallia is Gallo-Romance Vulgar Latin, and its positional table describes lenition in progress, not Old French spelling. Intervocalic ⟨v⟩ is /v/ in Old French, not [β] or [w] (§105); intervocalic /d/ survived as [ð] only until about the end of the 11th century and then fell (§116.1), so ⟨d⟩ between vowels in Old French text is not a dental fricative; and Latin CA- is spelled ⟨ch⟩ once it palatalises, leaving ⟨c⟩ before ⟨a⟩ as /k/. Those entries are declared here as this spec's own only where Old French supports them. Stress exemption: Old French word stress was inherited from Latin etymology (largely penultimate/antepenultimate by Latin rule) and is not recoverable from Old French spelling itself; no stress block is declared. Source: Pope, M. K. (1934), From Latin to Modern French, secs. on accentuation.
